Colour the Moser Spindle

Graph TheoryCoordinatesUnit Distance Problem
Game: Paint all seven dots so that two dots joined by a line never have the same colour.
How to play: Tap a dot to give it the next colour. A joined pair with the same colour glows red. First try with 4 colours, then with 3.

Look for the math

Each line joins two points exactly 1 apart. Two equilateral triangles form a rhombus; two rhombi share the point A, and they are turned about A just far enough that their far tips are also 1 apart. That is the Moser spindle, found by the brothers Leo and William Moser in 1961.

Why 3 colours fail

In a triangle all three points differ. In a rhombus (A, B, C, D, with B and C the middle points) B and C differ from each other, and A and D each differ from both of them. With only 3 colours, A and D must then both take the third one. That holds in each rhombus, so each far tip has the same colour as A. But the two tips D and D' are 1 apart and so must differ, while both match A. That is a contradiction. The test confirms it by trying every colouring: none of 37 works, and 4 colours do.

Colouring the plane

If a colouring of the whole plane gives different colours to points 1 apart, then it also colours this spindle properly, so the plane needs at least 4 colours. In 2018 Aubrey de Grey found a much larger unit-distance graph that needs 5, and seven colours (tiling the plane in small hexagons) are enough. Whether the answer is 5, 6 or 7 is the Hadwiger–Nelson problem, still open.

Link to the unit distance problem

The same graphs, points of the plane joined when 1 apart, are what the unit distance problem counts. One asks how few colours a unit distance graph needs, the other how many edges it can have.

Choose 3 colours and use "Is it possible?" Where does your attempt first get stuck?
